case.title: The August dip at Calder Quay Hotel
case.setting: Calder Quay Hotel is a 212-room, eight-floor four-star hotel in the fictional harbour city of Merrowby. A regional management group runs it. An external survey vendor collects its monthly Guest Satisfaction Score (GSS), and the score counts toward the leadership team's bonus. Floors 1-5 hold 128 rooms and floors 6-8 hold 84. Two changes went in this summer: a new self-check-in kiosk system on 23 June, and a new housekeeping contractor from 1 July.
case.presentingRequest: The Regional VP of Operations wants to know why the August GSS fell from 8.6 to 8.1 and what the hotel should do. She also wants answers on two specific questions: should the hotel give notice to the new housekeeping contractor, and should it pull the self-check-in kiosks?

initialEvidence.source: Email from Dana Okafor-Reyes, Regional VP Operations, to General Manager Tomasz Ellery, 2 September 2026
initialEvidence.text: Tomasz - August GSS came in at 8.1 against our 8.5 target, the first miss in fourteen months. We changed two things this summer: Orrin Facility Group took over housekeeping on 1 July, and the new self-check-in kiosks went live on 23 June. I've read a handful of the August comments and one on a booking site called the room 'tired and dusty'. Complaints logged at the desk are up roughly 40%. My view is that Orrin is the problem and we should serve notice before the 1 October renewal window closes. Please also tell me whether we need to pull the kiosks. I want a recommendation by Friday.

initialEvidence.source: Pellmore Insights GSS dashboard, monthly export for Calder Quay Hotel
initialEvidence.text: Questionnaire version Q7 (in use since January 2025, unchanged). Invitations go to every checked-out stay with a valid email address, as before. July: 412 responses, overall 8.6. August: 398 responses, overall 8.1. By floor block, July to August. Floors 1-5 (128 rooms; 241 August responses): overall 8.6 to 8.5; room comfort 8.4 to 8.3; cleanliness 8.7 to 8.7; check-in 8.8 to 8.8; value for money 8.0 to 7.7. Floors 6-8 (84 rooms; 157 August responses): overall 8.6 to 7.4; room comfort 8.4 to 6.1; cleanliness 8.7 to 8.6; check-in 8.8 to 8.7; value for money 8.0 to 7.3. Vendor note: for this property, month-to-month movements under 0.2 on any score fall within normal variation (trailing 18 months).

04 Aug 15:20 | Chiller CH-2 (east riser, serves floors 6-8) tripped on compressor fault. Reset failed. Guest calls about heat: 23 by 21:00. 05 Aug 09:40 | Contractor diagnosis: failed compressor contactor. Part not in stock; supplier lead time 11 working days. Portable units deployed to 12 rooms (all held). 07-18 Aug | Spot readings in occupied rooms on floors 6-8: 26.5-29.0 C (set point 22). 19 Aug 14:10 | Contactor fitted, CH-2 restored. Floors 6-8 below 23 C by 22:00. Notes: annual preventive maintenance on both CH-2 and CH-1 (west riser, floors 1-5) deferred in April 2026 under a budget hold; neither yet rescheduled. CH-1 has not faulted this year.

initialEvidence.source: Pellmore Insights daily view and verbatim tagging report, August 2026
initialEvidence.text: Floors 6-8 overall score by checkout date: 1-4 Aug 8.5 (n=19); 5-20 Aug 6.8 (n=96); 21-31 Aug 8.4 (n=42); 1-14 Sep 8.6 (n=71). Floors 1-5 daily scores stayed between 8.4 and 8.6 throughout August and early September. Verbatim tagging, August (vendor auto-tags, spot-checked by guest relations): 74 negative comments, 61 of them from floors 6-8. Heat / air conditioning / 'stuffy': 56, all floors 6-8. Cleanliness: 4 (July: 5), 2 per block. Check-in or kiosk: 2 (July: 3). Price or value: 6 (July: 2), 4 of them from floors 1-5. Other: 6.

initialEvidence.source: Rooms division monthly KPI pack, compiled by the Executive Housekeeper and Front Office Manager
initialEvidence.text: Room inspections are done by in-house supervisors, not by the contractor. Pass rate: June 95% (Linthwaite, prior contractor); July 96% (Orrin); August 95% (Orrin), with 95% on floors 1-5 and 95% on floors 6-8. About 640 inspections a month. Front-desk complaint log: July 50 entries, August 71. August by category (July in brackets): room temperature 24 (1); noise 11 (12); housekeeping 9 (10); billing 8 (9); kiosk/check-in 6 (7); other 13 (11). Share of guests checking in at kiosks: July 41%, August 43%. Average queue at peak: July 4.1 min, August 3.9 min.

initialEvidence.source: Note from Priya Vantongeren, Revenue Manager, to the General Manager, 3 September 2026
initialEvidence.text: 'Rack and BAR rates went up 6% hotel-wide from 1 August, as planned in the annual budget. We review rates weekly and can move them at any time. I can't tell you whether that hurt the value score. Value for money dips every August here: last year it went from 8.1 to 7.9 with no rate change, because of festival-season pricing across the city, and the overall score went from 8.5 to 8.4 last August as well. This year's value drop on floors 1-5 is slightly bigger, but nothing I have separates the rate rise from the usual seasonal dip.'

catalogue.title: Orrin Facility Group monthly service reports, July-August 2026
catalogue.text: Monthly service report to Calder Quay Hotel. July / August: rooms serviced 5,812 / 5,990; rooms released by 15:00 98% / 97%; self-audit quality score 97% / 97%; average attendants per shift 21 / 22; two attendant absences in August covered by agency staff. Report note: 'The client notified no service failures in either month. Several attendants reported very warm conditions on floors 6-8 during mid-August and were given extra breaks.'

catalogue.title: Front-office staffing rotas and overtime, June-August 2026
catalogue.text: Front-office rota summary. Headcount: June 18.0 FTE, July 18.5, August 18.0. Overtime hours: June 112, July 96, August 104. In July, two new agents completed kiosk and desk training. No peak-hour shifts went unfilled in July or August. A duty manager was on the rota every night in August.

catalogue.title: Self-check-in kiosk supplier support tickets, June-September 2026
catalogue.text: Support log for Calder Quay. 11 tickets since go-live on 23 June: 8 between 23 June and 6 July (key-card encoder calibration, receipt printer jams), 2 later in July (screen freeze, fixed by restart), 1 in August (receipt paper sensor). Kiosk availability: July 99.1%, August 99.6%. No tickets open at 31 August.

catalogue.title: Public review-site ratings and comments, July-August 2026
catalogue.source: Guest relations extract from public review sites
catalogue.text: July: 58 reviews, average 4.4/5. August: 63 reviews, average 4.1/5. August reviews mentioning heat, air conditioning or stuffy rooms: 19 (July: 0). Mentioning cleanliness or dust: 2 (July: 3). One of these is the 'tired and dusty' review, which also says the room was 'like an oven'. Mentioning check-in: 3 positive, 1 negative. Mentioning price: 3 (July: 2).

catalogue.title: Survey vendor methodology statement, 2026
catalogue.text: Invitations go out 24 hours after checkout to every stay with a valid email address; there is no sampling. Questionnaire version Q7 has been in use since January 2025 with no changes to wording, scale or order. Response rates: June 31%, July 31%, August 30%. The invitation template, timing and reminder schedule have not changed in 2026.

catalogue.title: Building management system corridor temperature trends, August 2026
catalogue.text: Hourly averages from floor 6-8 corridor sensors. 1-3 Aug: 21.8-22.6 C. 4 Aug: rising from 16:00. 6-18 Aug: daytime 27.4-30.2 C, overnight 25.9-27.1 C. 19 Aug: falls from 28.6 C at 14:00 to 22.9 C at 22:00. 20-31 Aug: 21.7-22.8 C. Floor 1-5 corridor sensors stayed at 21.5-23.0 C all through August.

catalogue.title: Guest compensation and room-move ledger, August 2026
catalogue.text: Guest recovery ledger, August. Room moves from floors 6-8 to floors 1-5: 14 (limited by 91% occupancy). Portable cooling units hired: 12, EUR 1,150. Goodwill credits to floor 6-8 stays between 4 and 19 August: 88 stays, EUR 7,920 in total, mostly one-night rate reductions. Credits for all other causes in August: EUR 640 (July: EUR 710).

catalogue.title: Competitive-set guest satisfaction benchmark, June-August 2026
catalogue.source: Merrowby hotel association shared survey programme
catalogue.text: Benchmark across five comparable four-star hotels in Merrowby (anonymised). Average overall guest satisfaction: June 8.4, July 8.4, August 8.3. None of the participating hotels reported a building-systems outage in August. The association does not publish individual hotels' pricing or rate changes.

catalogue.title: Municipal weather station daily records, August 2026
catalogue.text: Daily maximum temperatures: 1-5 Aug 24-27 C; 6-17 Aug 31-35 C (heat advisory 8-16 Aug); 18-31 Aug 23-28 C. The August mean maximum was 29.6 C, against a ten-year August average of 26.1 C.

catalogue.title: Housekeeping staff pulse survey, August 2026
catalogue.source: Anonymous pulse survey of Orrin attendants and in-house supervisors
catalogue.text: 27 responses from 41 invited. 'I have the supplies I need': 85% agree. 'My room quota is manageable': 52% agree (May, under Linthwaite: 49%). 'I am proud of the standard of rooms I hand over': 81% agree. Free-text themes: heat on the upper floors in August (9 mentions), uniform sizing (4), timing of linen deliveries (3).

catalogue.title: Rate change record and occupancy report, July-August 2026

Cleanliness scores were flat: 8.7 to 8.7 on floors 1-5 and 8.7 to 8.6 on floors 6-8, both inside the 0.2 noise band. The drop appears only on the floors CH-2 serves, and floors 1-5 act as a comparison group. The other explanations (front desk, housekeeping, survey changes) are ruled out. The score recovers after the repair, which serves as an on/off natural experiment.

The evidence counts against the link itself. After go-live, July scored a normal 8.6. Check-in scores were flat, kiosk complaints fell slightly, queues shortened, and the same kiosks serve floors 1-5, where scores did not drop.

But value for money falls every August, and a seasonal explanation is not ruled out. The revenue manager says nothing separates the two, so causation is not established. Nothing counts against the link, so 'contradicted' is not justified.

Cleanliness scores did not fall after the contractor change: 8.7 to 8.7 and 8.7 to 8.6. Independent in-house inspection pass rates are unchanged (June 95%, July 96%, August 95%). The evidence counts directly against the claimed effect.

CH-1, which serves floors 1-5, is on the same deferred status and has not been rescheduled. Reinstating maintenance, holding spares and setting a recovery protocol tackles the confirmed cause and the remaining exposure for all 212 rooms.

Cleanliness scores and independent inspections show the contractor is performing. Terminating the contract punishes the wrong party and disrupts housekeeping. It would cause damage whether the cooling explanation or the still-live rate explanation is true, because neither involves housekeeping.

case.setting: Calder Quay Hotel is a 212-room, eight-floor four-star hotel in the fictional harbour city of Merrowby. A regional management group runs it. An external survey vendor collects its monthly Guest Satisfaction Score (GSS), and the score counts toward the leadership team's bonus. Floors 1-5 hold 128 rooms and floors 6-8 hold 84. Two changes went in this summer: a new self-check-in kiosk system on 23 June, and a new housekeeping contractor from 1 July.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: The August GSS dip at Calder Quay came from a cooling failure, not from the two summer changes leadership suspects. On 4 August chiller CH-2, which serves only floors 6-8, failed when a compressor contactor wore out. The hotel had no spare because the annual preventive service, which normally comes with a spares kit, had been deferred in April under a budget hold. The replacement part took eleven working days, so rooms on floors 6-8 sat at 26.5-29 C until 19 August. Scores for floors 6-8 fell from 8.6 to 7.4, almost entirely in room comfort. Daily scores for those floors dropped only for checkouts during the outage and recovered once cooling was restored. Floors 1-5 share the same front desk, kiosks, housekeeping contractor and survey, and their overall score moved only within normal variation. Cleanliness, check-in, inspection pass rates, queue times and kiosk complaints were all flat. The 40% rise in desk complaints is explained by room-temperature complaints. The 6% rate rise coincides with a lower value-for-money score, but the same score falls every August in this festival city, and nothing in the evidence separates the two effects. CH-1, which serves floors 1-5, is still on deferred maintenance with no spare on site, so the same risk remains. The initial file establishes all of this, and every catalogue item only confirms it or is irrelevant.

answers.rationale: Several findings point the same way. The drop is confined to floors 6-8: 8.6 to 7.4 there, against 8.6 to 8.5 on floors 1-5. Those are the floors served by CH-2. On those floors room comfort fell from 8.4 to 6.1 while the other subscores stayed flat. Daily scores for floors 6-8 fall exactly during the 4-19 August outage and recover afterwards. 56 negative comments are about heat, all from floors 6-8. Weighting the floor blocks by response count reproduces the 8.1 hotel-wide figure.

The kiosks went live on 23 June, and July still scored a normal 8.6. The check-in subscore held at 8.8 on floors 1-5 and 8.7 on floors 6-8. Kiosk complaints went from 7 to 6, and peak queue time improved from 4.1 to 3.9 minutes. Both floor blocks use the same front desk, yet only floors 6-8 dropped.

Cleanliness scores were flat: 8.7 to 8.7 on floors 1-5 and 8.7 to 8.6 on floors 6-8, both inside the 0.2 noise band. In-house inspections, not the contractor's own audits, show pass rates of 95-96% before and after the contractor change, and the same on both floor blocks. Cleanliness comments went from 5 to 4. The single 'dusty' review cited by the VP is an anecdote, and the rise in desk complaints is made up of room-temperature complaints (24 against 1), not housekeeping complaints (9 against 10).

The vendor, the questionnaire version and the invitation rule are all unchanged, and response counts are similar (412 and 398). A change to how the survey was administered would affect every floor, but the drop is confined to the floors that lost cooling and reverses after the repair.

On floors 1-5 the overall score fell by 0.1, which is within normal variation, and value for money fell by 0.3. Last August, with no rate change, value fell by 0.2 and the overall score by 0.1. The extra 0.1 this year is below the vendor's noise threshold. The evidence neither establishes a contribution from the rate rise nor rules one out, and no catalogue item separates rate from season.

All the elements of a causal case are present. The outage begins before the score falls. The mechanism is documented: rooms at 26.5-29 C and comments about heat. The drop appears only on the floors CH-2 serves, and floors 1-5 act as a comparison group. The other explanations (front desk, housekeeping, survey changes) are ruled out. The score recovers after the repair, which serves as an on/off natural experiment.

The evidence counts against the link itself. After go-live, July scored a normal 8.6. Check-in scores were flat, kiosk complaints fell slightly, queues shortened, and the same kiosks serve floors 1-5, where scores did not drop.

The rate rise and the lower value score occur together, and price comments rose from 2 to 6, so there is an association. But value for money falls every August, and a seasonal explanation is not ruled out. The revenue manager says nothing separates the two, so causation is not established. Nothing counts against the link, so 'contradicted' is not justified.

Cleanliness scores did not fall after the contractor change: 8.7 to 8.7 and 8.7 to 8.6. Independent in-house inspection pass rates are unchanged (June 95%, July 96%, August 95%). The evidence counts directly against the claimed effect.

Cooling failure is the established cause. The outage lasted 15 days because no spare part was held after the maintenance deferral. CH-1, which serves floors 1-5, is on the same deferred status and has not been rescheduled. Reinstating maintenance, holding spares and setting a recovery protocol tackles the confirmed cause and the remaining exposure for all 212 rooms.

Cleanliness scores and independent inspections show the contractor is performing. Terminating the contract punishes the wrong party and disrupts housekeeping. It would cause damage whether the cooling explanation or the still-live rate explanation is true, because neither involves housekeeping.

If the rate rise were shown to depress value ratings, reversing it would help recover them. Rates are reviewed weekly and can be moved at any time, so a reversal could be undone. But whether the rate rise had any effect beyond the usual seasonal dip is unconfirmed, so committing to a reversal now is not justified.

Goodwill outreach to the guests who were affected is reasonable and low-risk. It deals only with past harm, though. Unlike A1, it does nothing about the deferred maintenance and missing spares that leave both risers exposed to a repeat.

Removing real guest responses suppresses the signal of an operational failure and distorts a bonus-linked metric. It is harmful under every hypothesis, because no explanation makes those responses invalid.

The initial file establishes the cooling cause, rules out the housekeeping, kiosk and survey explanations, documents the deferred maintenance on both chillers, and shows the rate question cannot be settled. That is enough to commit to A1. No catalogue item changes any answer.

(1) The 40% rise in desk complaints is answered by E5's category breakdown (temperature complaints 24 against 1). (2) The 'tired and dusty' review is answered by flat cleanliness scores and independent inspections; C4 adds that the same review also says the room was 'like an oven', which only confirms. (3) The kiosk suspicion is answered by July's normal score after the June go-live, flat check-in scores and shorter queues. The floor-block split in E2 acts as a built-in comparison group, and the daily on/off series in E4 serves as a natural experiment. The rate question (H5/R3) is deliberately left undecidable by the whole catalogue: C8 gives competitor overall scores but no competitor pricing, C11 says the revenue system holds no satisfaction data, and C14 has one anecdotal price complaint. Several catalogue items (C6, C7, C12, C15) are attractive confirmatory reads, but they repeat facts already in E3 and E4. Arithmetic check: (241 x 8.5 + 157 x 7.4) / 398 = 8.07, which rounds to 8.1. Floor 6-8 daily series: (19 x 8.5 + 96 x 6.8 + 42 x 8.4) / 157 = 7.43. Complaint categories sum to 71 (August) and 50 (July). Verbatim tags sum to 74, with 61 from floors 6-8.
